rv.q: Elektra draws its centrifugal power from the harmony at its core, and the harshly beautiful, straight-tone Balkan belt of these six vocalists pierces as brazenly as Elektra’s own howling in the darkness.
The acting ensemble is uniformly dynamic.
The ensemble delivers Carson’s sharp-edged, propulsive verse with an unadorned clarity.
Overall, though, Mr. Fish’s interpretation may leave you more mystified than entertained.
Daniel Fish’s Elektra, on the other hand, has been drained of all its power.
Elektra is a frustrating experience because there’s so much here that’s compelling without the directorial overreach.
Fish’s work is always mind-blowing, but with Elektra, that is both positive and negative.

cn.t: Critics are divided on Daniel Fish's stark, concept-heavy *Elektra*—Tina Benko's fierce performance and Ted Hearne's a cappella score earn praise, but Fish's modern impositions on Sophocles feel heavy-handed to some.
